lessons.title: What Are Mobile Apps
lessons.content: A mobile app is software for smartphones and tablets. Native apps are built for one platform (Android: Kotlin/Java, iOS: Swift) — fast with full device access. Cross-platform apps (Flutter, React Native) use one codebase for both — faster to develop. Web apps run in browsers. Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) can be installed and work offline. Choose based on: target audience, budget, features needed, and timeline.
examples: Instagram is native — separate code for Android and iOS
Flutter: one Dart codebase runs on Android, iOS, Windows, and web
Twitter's PWA can be installed from the browser

keyTerms.native app: Built for one platform using its native language
keyTerms.PWA: Progressive Web App — installable web app with offline support
keyTerms.SDK: Software Development Kit — tools and libraries for building apps

quiz.question: Main advantage of cross-platform:
quiz.explanation: Write once, deploy everywhere.

quiz.question: Native Android language:
quiz.explanation: Kotlin (and Java) for Android.

quiz.question: PWA differs from regular website by:
options: Can be installed and works offline
quiz.explanation: PWAs cache content for offline use and can be installed.

quiz.question: Flutter uses which language?
quiz.explanation: Flutter apps are written in Dart.

quiz.question: When to choose native over cross-platform:
options: When you need maximum performance and full platform features
When speed of development is priority
quiz.explanation: Native gives best performance and full access to platform-specific features.

lessons.title: UI/UX Design Principles
lessons.content: UI (User Interface) is how the app looks — buttons, colors, text. UX (User Experience) is how it feels to use. Principles: consistency (same patterns throughout), feedback (app responds to every action), simplicity, accessibility (usable by people with disabilities). Use established patterns: bottom nav bars, pull to refresh, swipe gestures. Material Design (Android) and Human Interface Guidelines (iOS) provide platform-specific design standards. Always test with real users.
examples: Loading spinner gives feedback — user knows something is happening
Bottom nav (Home, Search, Profile) — a pattern users already know
High contrast text ensures readability for all users

keyTerms.UX: User Experience — ease and pleasantness of use
keyTerms.Material Design: Google's design system for Android apps
keyTerms.wireframe: A low-fidelity sketch of an app's layout before coding

quiz.question: UI vs UX:
options: UI is looks, UX is feel
UI is backend, UX is frontend
UI is mobile, UX is web
quiz.explanation: UI = visual design, UX = overall experience.

quiz.question: Consistency is important because:
options: Users learn patterns once and apply everywhere
quiz.explanation: Consistent design reduces cognitive load.

quiz.question: Accessibility means:
quiz.explanation: Everyone should be able to use the app.

quiz.question: A wireframe is:
options: A low-fidelity sketch of app layout
quiz.explanation: Wireframes plan layout before investing in full design.

quiz.question: Material Design is:
quiz.explanation: Material Design provides components, patterns, and guidelines for Android apps.

lessons.title: App Architecture Patterns
lessons.content: Architecture organizes app code. MVC: Model (data), View (display), Controller (logic). MVVM: ViewModel prepares data for View and handles actions — popular in modern apps. Clean Architecture separates: presentation (UI), domain (business logic), data (databases, APIs). State management tracks what the app shows. Good architecture means easier testing, debugging, and extending. Separation of concerns: each part does one job.
examples: View: login screen with fields and button
Model: User object with name, email, photo
ViewModel: validates input, calls API, tells View the result

keyTerms.state management: Tracking what the app displays at any moment
keyTerms.MVVM: Model-View-ViewModel — modern pattern for reactive UI updates

quiz.question: In MVC, View does:
quiz.explanation: View is the UI layer.

quiz.question: State management matters because:
options: It tracks what the app should display
quiz.explanation: UI must always reflect current data and user actions.

quiz.question: Separation of concerns means:
quiz.explanation: Each module does one job — UI doesn't mix with data logic.

quiz.question: MVVM is popular because:
options: ViewModel automatically updates the View when data changes
quiz.explanation: MVVM enables reactive UI — View observes ViewModel and updates automatically.

quiz.question: Clean Architecture layers are:
quiz.explanation: Presentation (UI) → Domain (business logic) → Data (storage/network).

lessons.title: Development Environment Setup
lessons.content: Before building apps, you need the right tools. For Flutter: install Flutter SDK, Android Studio (or VS Code with Flutter extension), and set up an Android emulator or connect a physical device. For React Native: install Node.js, a code editor, and Expo (simplifies setup). Android development requires the Android SDK and JDK. iOS development requires a Mac with Xcode. Version control: install Git from day one. Use a code editor with good extensions: syntax highlighting, code completion, linting, and debugging tools. Hot reload (Flutter, React Native) lets you see changes instantly without restarting the app — dramatically speeds up development.
examples: Flutter setup: download SDK → add to PATH → run 'flutter doctor' to check everything is ready
Android Studio provides: code editor, emulator, debugger, and SDK management all in one
Hot reload: change a button color → save → see the change on your phone in under 1 second

keyTerms.SDK: Software Development Kit — tools and libraries needed to build apps
keyTerms.emulator: A virtual device that simulates a phone on your computer
keyTerms.hot reload: Instantly see code changes in the running app without restarting
keyTerms.IDE: Integrated Development Environment — code editor with built-in tools

quiz.question: Flutter's 'flutter doctor' command:
options: Checks if your development environment is properly set up
quiz.explanation: flutter doctor diagnoses your setup — reporting missing tools or configuration.

quiz.question: Hot reload is useful because:
options: See changes instantly without restarting the app
quiz.explanation: Hot reload drastically speeds up development — tweak UI and see results in under a second.

quiz.question: iOS development requires:
quiz.explanation: Apple requires Xcode (Mac only) to build and submit iOS apps.

quiz.question: An emulator is:
options: A virtual device simulating a phone on your computer
quiz.explanation: Emulators let you test apps without a physical device.

quiz.question: Why install Git on day one?
options: Track all code changes from the start — undo mistakes, collaborate, backup
Git is required to run apps
quiz.explanation: Version control from day one means you can always go back if something breaks.

lessons.title: Planning Your First App
lessons.content: Before writing code, plan your app. Define the problem: what specific problem does your app solve? Who are your users? List features and prioritize: MVP (Minimum Viable Product) includes only essential features — launch fast, get feedback, then improve. Create user stories: 'As a student, I want to track my homework so I don't forget assignments.' Design screens: sketch wireframes on paper first — it's faster than coding. Define the data model: what information does the app store? (users, tasks, settings). Choose your tech stack: framework, database, backend. Plan navigation: how do users move between screens? Start simple — a working simple app is better than an unfinished complex one.
examples: MVP for a todo app: add tasks, mark complete, delete — that's it. Sorting, categories, and reminders come later
User story: 'As a farmer, I want to photograph my crop and get disease diagnosis so I can treat it early'
Data model for a school app: Students(name, grade), Assignments(title, due_date, subject), Scores(student_id, assignment_id, score)

keyTerms.MVP: Minimum Viable Product — the simplest version with only core features
keyTerms.user story: A description of a feature from the user's perspective
keyTerms.wireframe: A simple sketch of the app's screens and layout
keyTerms.tech stack: The combination of technologies used to build the app

quiz.question: An MVP should include:
options: Only essential core features — launch fast, improve later
quiz.explanation: MVP = minimum features to solve the core problem. Get feedback, then add more.

quiz.question: User stories are written from:
quiz.explanation: 'As a [user], I want [feature] so that [benefit]' — always user-focused.

quiz.question: Why sketch wireframes before coding?
options: Changing a sketch is faster and cheaper than changing code
quiz.explanation: Paper prototyping catches design problems early — before investing hours in code.

quiz.question: A data model defines:
options: What information the app stores and how it's structured
quiz.explanation: Data models plan the entities (users, posts, messages) and their relationships.

quiz.question: Starting simple is better because:
options: A working simple app beats an unfinished complex one
quiz.explanation: Ship something working, get real user feedback, then iterate and improve.

lessons.title: Widgets and Components
lessons.content: Everything on screen is a widget (Flutter) or component (React Native). Widgets are reusable UI blocks — buttons, text, images, cards. They nest to build complex layouts: Screen → Column → Card → Text + Image. Stateless widgets display fixed content. Stateful widgets change based on interaction. Build apps by composing small widgets into larger ones — like LEGO.
examples: Text('Hello World') — displays text
Column(children: [Text('Title'), Text('Subtitle')]) — vertical layout
ElevatedButton(onPressed: login, child: Text('Log In')) — clickable button

keyTerms.stateful: Can change based on user interaction
keyTerms.composition: Building complex UI by nesting smaller widgets together

quiz.question: A widget is:
quiz.explanation: Widgets are the fundamental UI elements.

quiz.question: Use stateful widget when:
options: UI needs to change based on user action
quiz.explanation: Stateful rebuilds when state changes.

quiz.question: Complex layouts are built by:
quiz.explanation: Compose smaller widgets into larger structures.

quiz.question: A StatelessWidget in Flutter:
options: Never changes once built — no internal state
quiz.explanation: Stateless = immutable. For dynamic content, use StatefulWidget.

quiz.question: The build() method:
options: Describes what the widget looks like
quiz.explanation: build() returns the widget tree describing this component's UI.

lessons.title: Layouts and Navigation
lessons.content: Row arranges horizontally, Column vertically, Stack layers on top. ListView creates scrollable lists, GridView creates grids. Navigation moves between screens. Patterns: bottom nav bar (3-5 tabs), drawer (hamburger menu), stack navigation (push/pop screens). Deep linking opens specific screens from URLs or notifications. Use named routes for clean navigation: Navigator.pushNamed(context, '/details').
examples: Row(children: [Icon(star), Text('Favorite')])
Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => DetailScreen()))
BottomNavigationBar with Home, Search, Profile tabs

keyTerms.deep linking: Opening specific screens from external URLs or notifications
keyTerms.route: A named path to a screen in the app

quiz.question: Column arranges items:
quiz.explanation: Column = top to bottom.

quiz.question: Bottom nav bar is for:
quiz.explanation: Quick access to 3-5 main sections.

quiz.question: Stack navigation works like:
options: Deck of cards — push new, pop to go back
quiz.explanation: Push adds screen on top; pop reveals previous.

quiz.question: ListView is used when:
options: Content is too long to fit on screen and needs scrolling
quiz.explanation: ListView handles scrollable lists of any length efficiently.

quiz.question: Deep linking allows:
options: Opening a specific screen from a URL or notification
quiz.explanation: Users can jump directly to specific content within the app.

lessons.title: Handling User Input
lessons.content: Text fields collect typed text — validate input (valid email? strong password?). Buttons trigger actions. Gesture detectors handle swipes, long presses, drags. Forms group inputs and validate together before submitting. Show feedback: loading indicators, success messages, error states. Handle keyboard: show/hide appropriately, don't let it cover inputs. Debounce search inputs — wait until user stops typing before searching.
examples: TextField with validation: if email doesn't contain @, show error
SnackBar after saving: 'Profile updated!'
Debounce: search triggers 300ms after user stops typing, not on every keystroke

keyTerms.gesture: Touch interaction: tap, swipe, long press
keyTerms.debounce: Delaying an action until user stops performing it (typing, scrolling)

quiz.question: Validate input to:
options: Ensure data is correct before processing
quiz.explanation: Catch errors early, ensure data quality.

quiz.question: A gesture is:
options: Touch interaction like tap or swipe
quiz.explanation: Touch-based: tap, swipe, long press, pinch.

quiz.question: While data is loading, show:
quiz.explanation: Users need feedback that something is happening.

quiz.question: Debouncing search means:
options: Waiting until user stops typing before searching
quiz.explanation: Debounce reduces unnecessary API calls — only search when typing pauses.

quiz.question: Form validation should happen:
options: Before submitting — show errors inline next to fields
After data is sent to server only
quiz.explanation: Client-side validation gives instant feedback — server-side is also needed for security.

lessons.title: Lists and Dynamic Content
lessons.content: Most apps display lists of data: messages, products, contacts, feeds. In Flutter, ListView.builder creates lists efficiently — it only builds visible items (lazy loading). Each item needs a unique key for efficient updates. Pull-to-refresh lets users reload data by pulling down. Pagination loads data in chunks: load 20 items, when user scrolls near the bottom, load 20 more. Empty states: when a list has no data, show a helpful message ('No messages yet — start a conversation!'). Loading states: show skeletons or shimmer effects while data loads. Error states: show a retry button if loading fails.
examples: ListView.builder(itemCount: items.length, itemBuilder: (ctx, i) => ListTile(title: Text(items[i].name)))
Pull-to-refresh: RefreshIndicator(onRefresh: loadData, child: ListView(...))
Empty state: if (items.isEmpty) return Center(child: Text('No items yet'))

keyTerms.lazy loading: Only building/loading items that are currently visible on screen
keyTerms.pagination: Loading data in chunks as the user scrolls through
keyTerms.empty state: UI shown when a list has no data — guides the user on what to do
keyTerms.skeleton screen: A placeholder loading UI showing the shape of content before data arrives

quiz.question: ListView.builder is efficient because:
options: It only builds items currently visible on screen
quiz.explanation: Lazy building means only visible items consume memory and processing.

quiz.question: Why does each list item need a unique key?
options: For efficient updates — framework knows which items changed
quiz.explanation: Keys help the framework identify, update, and reorder items efficiently.

quiz.question: Pagination improves performance by:
options: Loading data in small chunks instead of everything at once
quiz.explanation: Loading 20 items at a time is much faster than loading 10,000.

quiz.question: An empty state should:
options: Guide the user on what to do next
quiz.explanation: Empty states help users: 'No projects yet — tap + to create one.'

quiz.question: Skeleton screens are:
options: Placeholder shapes shown while real content loads
quiz.explanation: Skeletons show the layout shape with gray placeholders — feels faster than a spinner.

lessons.title: Responsive and Adaptive UI
lessons.content: Apps run on many screen sizes: small phones, large phones, tablets, and desktops. Responsive UI adapts layout to screen size. Use MediaQuery to get screen dimensions. LayoutBuilder provides parent constraints. Flexible and Expanded widgets distribute space proportionally. For different layouts: use breakpoints — phone shows single column, tablet shows two columns, desktop shows sidebar + content. Platform-adaptive means adjusting to the platform's conventions: Android uses Material Design (bottom nav, FABs), iOS uses Cupertino (tab bars, sliding panels). Consider orientation: portrait vs landscape may need different layouts.
examples: if (MediaQuery.of(context).size.width > 600) showSidebar() else showBottomNav()
Flexible(flex: 2, child: mainContent), Flexible(flex: 1, child: sidebar) — 2:1 ratio
OrientationBuilder detects portrait/landscape and adjusts layout accordingly

keyTerms.responsive: UI that adapts its layout to different screen sizes
keyTerms.adaptive: UI that adjusts to platform conventions (Material on Android, Cupertino on iOS)
keyTerms.breakpoint: A screen width threshold where the layout changes
keyTerms.MediaQuery: Flutter tool providing screen size, orientation, and other device info

quiz.question: Responsive design means:
options: Layout adapts to different screen sizes
quiz.explanation: Responsive UIs rearrange content to fit any screen size optimally.

quiz.question: A breakpoint is:
options: A screen width where the layout changes
quiz.explanation: Below 600px → phone layout. Above 600px → tablet layout. These thresholds are breakpoints.

quiz.question: Platform-adaptive means:
quiz.explanation: Android users expect Material Design; iOS users expect Cupertino style.

quiz.question: Expanded widget:
options: Takes up remaining available space in a Row/Column
quiz.explanation: Expanded fills whatever space is left after fixed-size siblings are placed.

quiz.question: Why consider landscape orientation?
options: Users may rotate their device — layout should still work well
quiz.explanation: Content that works in portrait may need rearranging for the wider landscape layout.

lessons.title: Local Data Storage
lessons.content: SharedPreferences for simple key-value pairs (settings). SQLite for structured data (profiles, records). File storage for large files (images, exports). Choose the right tool: settings → key-value, records → SQLite, files → file system. Handle first-launch (no data yet). Don't store large files in SQLite.
examples: SharedPreferences: isDarkMode = true
SQLite: student profiles with name, age, grade, history
File storage: save PDF certificate to documents

keyTerms.SQLite: Lightweight local database for structured data
keyTerms.local storage: Storing data on device, available offline
keyTerms.CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic data operations

quiz.question: Store theme preference in:
quiz.explanation: Simple settings → key-value storage.

quiz.question: Use SQLite for:
quiz.explanation: SQLite handles tables, rows, queries.

quiz.question: Local storage importance:
quiz.explanation: Offline, fast, and no server costs.

quiz.question: CRUD stands for:
quiz.explanation: The four fundamental database operations.

quiz.question: First-launch handling means:
options: Showing onboarding or defaults when there's no saved data yet
quiz.explanation: First-time users have no saved data — show setup/onboarding instead of empty screens.

lessons.title: State Management
lessons.content: State is the app's current data — which screen, logged-in user, cart items. Local state: one widget (text field value). Global state: shared across app (user profile, theme). Solutions: setState (simple), Provider/Riverpod (recommended), BLoC (enterprise). Key principle: state changes → UI rebuilds automatically. One-way data flow: action → state update → UI rebuild.
examples: Local: counter tracks its own count
Global: logged-in user available on every screen
Cart icon badge updates across app when item added

keyTerms.state: Current data and conditions of the app
keyTerms.Provider: State management making data available throughout widget tree
keyTerms.reactive: UI automatically updates when state changes
keyTerms.one-way data flow: Actions update state, state drives UI — predictable and debuggable

quiz.question: State is:
options: Current data the app is using
quiz.explanation: Everything the app currently knows and displays.

quiz.question: Use global state when:
quiz.explanation: User profile, theme, cart — needed in many places.

quiz.question: Reactive state means:
options: UI rebuilds automatically when state changes
quiz.explanation: Change state → UI updates without manual intervention.

quiz.question: setState is best for:
options: Simple local state within a single widget
quiz.explanation: setState works for simple cases; Provider/Riverpod for shared state.

quiz.question: One-way data flow means:
quiz.explanation: Unidirectional flow makes state changes predictable and debuggable.

lessons.title: Working with APIs
lessons.content: APIs let apps communicate with servers. REST uses HTTP: GET (retrieve), POST (send), PUT (update), DELETE (remove). Data in JSON. Make requests: send URL + parameters, wait for response, parse JSON. Handle errors: no internet, server down, invalid data. Show loading states. Cache responses for offline use. Use environment variables for API URLs — don't hardcode them.
examples: GET weather data → display temperature
POST login with email/password → receive auth token
Parse JSON: {'name': 'Alice', 'score': 95} → create Student object

keyTerms.API: Interface for apps to communicate with servers
keyTerms.authentication: Verifying user identity — usually with tokens

quiz.question: GET retrieves:
quiz.explanation: GET = retrieve without modifying.

quiz.question: API data format:
quiz.explanation: JSON is the standard for APIs.

quiz.question: Cache API responses to:
quiz.explanation: Cached data is available without internet.

quiz.question: Authentication tokens should be:
options: Stored securely, never in plain text or source code
quiz.explanation: Tokens are credentials — expose them and anyone can access user data.

quiz.question: When an API call fails, the app should:
options: Show an error message with a retry option
quiz.explanation: Graceful error handling: inform the user and offer a way to retry.

lessons.title: Push Notifications
lessons.content: Push notifications alert users even when the app isn't open. They drive engagement: reminders, messages, updates, promotions. Implementation: Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for both Android and iOS. Notification types: data (processed silently by the app) and display (shown to user with title, body, icon). Users must grant permission. Don't spam — respect user attention. Personalize: send relevant notifications based on user preferences and behavior. Schedule local notifications for reminders without a server. Handle notification taps — deep link to the relevant screen.
examples: 'You have a new lesson available: Introduction to Fractions' — tapping opens the lesson
Local notification: 'Time to study! You haven't practiced in 2 days' — scheduled on device
Silent data notification: sync new curriculum content in the background

keyTerms.push notification: Message sent to a user's device even when the app isn't open
keyTerms.FCM: Firebase Cloud Messaging — Google's service for sending push notifications
keyTerms.deep linking: Notification tap opens a specific screen within the app
keyTerms.local notification: Notification scheduled on the device without needing a server

quiz.question: Push notifications work when:
options: The app isn't open — they arrive at the system level
quiz.explanation: Push notifications reach users even when the app is closed or in background.

quiz.question: FCM stands for:
quiz.explanation: FCM is Google's cross-platform notification service.

quiz.question: Too many notifications will:
options: Annoy users and they'll disable them or uninstall
quiz.explanation: Respect user attention — send only relevant, valuable notifications.

quiz.question: Local notifications differ from push because:
options: They're scheduled on the device without a server
quiz.explanation: Local notifications are set by the app itself — no server or internet needed.

quiz.question: When a user taps a notification, the app should:
quiz.explanation: Deep linking to the relevant content gives users what they expected from the notification.

lessons.title: Offline-First Architecture
lessons.content: Offline-first means the app works without internet and syncs when connection returns. This is critical in areas with unreliable connectivity. Strategy: store all data locally first, then sync to server when online. Use a local database (SQLite, Hive) as the primary data source. Queue changes made offline and replay them when online. Handle conflicts: what if the same data was changed offline by two devices? Strategies include 'last write wins' or manual conflict resolution. Show connectivity status to users. Cache API responses. Prefetch content users will likely need. The best offline apps feel the same whether connected or not.
examples: A note-taking app: create notes offline → they sync to cloud when WiFi returns
Otic Studio: curriculum content is bundled in the app — works without any internet
Conflict resolution: user edited a document on phone and laptop offline → show both versions and let user choose

keyTerms.offline-first: Designing apps to work fully without internet, syncing when connected
keyTerms.sync: Transferring local changes to a server and vice versa when online
keyTerms.conflict resolution: Handling cases where the same data was changed in different places
keyTerms.queue: Storing pending operations to be executed when connection returns

quiz.question: Offline-first means:
options: App works without internet, syncs when connected
quiz.explanation: The app functions fully offline — internet is used for syncing, not for basic operation.

quiz.question: Why is offline-first important in developing countries?
options: Internet connectivity is often unreliable or unavailable
Offline apps are cheaper to build
quiz.explanation: Many users have intermittent or no connectivity — apps must work without it.

quiz.question: When offline changes sync, conflicts can occur when:
options: The same data was modified on multiple devices
quiz.explanation: Two devices editing the same record offline creates a conflict when both sync.

quiz.question: Queuing offline changes means:
options: Storing operations to replay when internet returns
quiz.explanation: Changes are saved locally and sent to the server in order when connection is restored.

quiz.question: The best offline apps:
options: Feel the same whether connected or not
quiz.explanation: Users shouldn't notice the difference — offline/online transitions should be seamless.

lessons.title: Testing Your App
lessons.content: Unit tests check individual functions. Widget tests verify UI components. Integration tests check complete flows. Test on real devices — emulators miss touch and performance issues. Test edge cases: empty input, no internet, long text, rapid tapping. Beta testing: give to real users before launch. Automated testing saves time — run tests with every code change.
examples: expect(add(2, 3), equals(5)) — unit test
Tap button → verify dialog appears — widget test
Give 20 users the app for a week → collect feedback

keyTerms.test coverage: Percentage of code covered by automated tests

quiz.question: Unit tests check:
quiz.explanation: Unit tests verify individual functions.

quiz.question: Test on real devices because:
options: Emulators miss touch and performance issues
quiz.explanation: Real devices show actual performance.

quiz.question: Beta testing is:
options: Pre-release to real users for feedback
quiz.explanation: Real users find bugs you missed.

quiz.question: Test coverage of 80% means:
options: 80% of code is tested by automated tests
quiz.explanation: Coverage measures how much code your tests exercise — aim for 70-90%.

quiz.question: Regression testing means:
options: Checking that new changes didn't break existing features
quiz.explanation: After every change, verify nothing that used to work is now broken.

lessons.title: App Store Publishing
lessons.content: Google Play: developer account ($25 one-time), prepare assets (icon, screenshots, description), build signed release, fill store listing, submit for review. Apple App Store: Apple Developer ($99/year), Mac with Xcode required. Version numbering: 1.0.0 (first release), 1.1.0 (features), 1.0.1 (bug fix). Privacy policy required. App Store Optimization (ASO): keywords in title and description help users find your app.
examples: Play Store needs: 512x512 icon, 2+ screenshots, descriptions
Version: major.minor.patch — 1.0.0 → 1.1.0 → 1.1.1
Privacy policy: explain what data you collect and how

keyTerms.store listing: App store page with screenshots and description
keyTerms.ASO: App Store Optimization — making your app discoverable in search

quiz.question: Google Play dev account costs:
quiz.explanation: One-time $25 fee.

quiz.question: App Bundle is:
options: Optimized format delivering only what each device needs
quiz.explanation: Google generates optimized APKs per device.

quiz.question: iOS publishing needs:
quiz.explanation: Mac + Xcode + Apple Developer account.

quiz.question: ASO helps with:
options: Making your app easier to find in the store
quiz.explanation: Keywords, good screenshots, and clear descriptions improve discoverability.

quiz.question: Semantic versioning 2.3.1 means:
quiz.explanation: Major (breaking changes), minor (new features), patch (bug fixes).

lessons.title: App Maintenance and Updates
lessons.content: Publishing isn't the end. Monitor crashes (Firebase Crashlytics). Read reviews and respond. Fix bugs promptly. Plan regular updates: performance, features, OS compatibility. Use analytics to understand usage. A/B testing compares feature versions. Monitor app size — keep it lean. Deprecation: remove old features gracefully with user notice.
examples: Crashlytics: 50 users crashed on login — null pointer line 42
Analytics: 80% never open Settings — move options elsewhere
A/B test: blue vs green button — green gets 15% more clicks

keyTerms.A/B testing: Comparing two versions to find which performs better
keyTerms.deprecation: Phasing out old features with advance notice to users

quiz.question: Monitor crashes to:
options: Find and fix bugs users experience
quiz.explanation: Fix issues before more users are affected.

quiz.question: A/B testing is:
options: Comparing two versions for better performance
quiz.explanation: Show different versions, measure which works better.

quiz.question: Keep updating because:
options: Fix bugs, add features, stay compatible
quiz.explanation: Regular updates maintain quality and compatibility.

quiz.question: App analytics help you:
options: Understand how users actually use the app and make data-driven decisions
quiz.explanation: Analytics reveal what features are popular and where users struggle.

quiz.question: When deprecating a feature:
options: Give users advance notice and time to adjust
Only remove it for new users
quiz.explanation: Warn users before removing features — give time to migrate or adapt.

lessons.title: App Security
lessons.content: Security protects user data and prevents attacks. Store sensitive data encrypted — never in plain text. Use HTTPS for all network communication. Authenticate users with secure tokens (JWT), not by sending passwords with each request. Validate all input — prevent injection attacks. Obfuscate your code in release builds to make reverse engineering harder. Don't store API keys or secrets in source code — use environment variables. Implement certificate pinning to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. Follow the principle of least privilege: request only the permissions your app actually needs. Regular security audits identify vulnerabilities before attackers do.
examples: Bad: storing password as plain text in SharedPreferences. Good: storing a hashed token
HTTPS encrypts data in transit — even on public WiFi, attackers can't read it
Obfuscation: release build changes meaningful names (getUserData) to meaningless ones (a.b()) — harder to reverse engineer

keyTerms.encryption: Converting data into unreadable format that can only be decoded with a key
keyTerms.HTTPS: Secure HTTP — encrypts communication between app and server
keyTerms.JWT: JSON Web Token — a secure token for authenticating API requests
keyTerms.obfuscation: Making code harder to understand if decompiled — protects intellectual property

quiz.question: Sensitive data should be stored:
options: In plain text for easy access
quiz.explanation: Plain text data can be read by anyone who accesses the device or database.

quiz.question: HTTPS protects against:
options: Data being read during transmission (man-in-the-middle attacks)
quiz.explanation: HTTPS encrypts the connection — attackers on the same network can't read the data.

quiz.question: API keys should be:
options: In environment variables, not in source code
quiz.explanation: Keys in source code are visible to anyone who decompiles the app.

quiz.question: Principle of least privilege means:
options: Only request permissions the app actually needs
quiz.explanation: Don't ask for camera, location, and contacts if you only need storage.

quiz.question: Code obfuscation:
options: Makes decompiled code harder to understand
quiz.explanation: Obfuscation renames variables and methods to meaningless names — harder to reverse engineer.

lessons.title: Monetization and Growth
lessons.content: How to make money from your app: freemium (basic free, premium paid), subscriptions (monthly/yearly recurring), in-app purchases (unlock features, content), advertising (show ads — use AdMob), paid apps (one-time purchase), and sponsorships. Choose based on your users and content type. Growth strategies: App Store Optimization (ASO), social media marketing, content marketing (blog/YouTube), referral programs ('invite a friend, both get premium'), and partnerships. Measure key metrics: DAU/MAU (daily/monthly active users), retention rate (% who return), LTV (lifetime value per user), and CAC (cost to acquire a customer). Retention is more important than acquisition — keeping existing users costs less than getting new ones.
examples: Freemium: basic learning free, advanced courses require premium ($4.99/month)
Referral: 'Share Otic Studio with a friend — you both get 1 month of premium free!'
Retention metric: 40% of users return after 7 days = good for educational apps

keyTerms.freemium: Basic features free, premium features require payment
keyTerms.retention rate: Percentage of users who continue using the app over time
keyTerms.LTV: Lifetime Value — total revenue a user generates over their entire time using the app
keyTerms.ASO: App Store Optimization — improving visibility in app store search results

quiz.question: Freemium means:
quiz.explanation: Users get value for free; those who want more pay for premium features.

quiz.question: Retention is more important than acquisition because:
options: Keeping existing users is cheaper than getting new ones
quiz.explanation: It costs 5-7x more to acquire a new user than to retain an existing one.

quiz.question: DAU/MAU measures:
options: How many users actively use the app daily/monthly
quiz.explanation: Daily/Monthly Active Users shows real engagement, not just downloads.

quiz.question: Best monetization for an educational app:
options: Freemium or subscription — users try before paying
quiz.explanation: Let students experience value first, then offer premium for advanced content.

quiz.question: A referral program works by:
options: Rewarding users who invite friends — both benefit
quiz.explanation: Word of mouth is the most trusted marketing — incentivize users to share.
